#### H · D46's reader half — the decision, made rather than deferred

The writer closed in WP 3.2: an unrecognised `time_unit` is refused at ingestion
and lands no value. The reader did not. `combine-project`'s resolver mapped every
unrecognised token to weekly with no finding anywhere, and §15 counts **27 such
tokens already in tier 2** — `21`, `15`, `16`, `7`, `14`, `9`, `4` and twenty
more, across six projects — each almost certainly a lead time in days that landed
one column left. A number whose source is a parse failure, displayed as data:
§5 T1 has no fourth option, and T2 says the substitution must be visible.

**The decision: compute, and say so. Not refuse, and not assume.**

Refusing would blank rows in projects whose owners did not cause the defect and
cannot fix it without re-uploading — destroying data to punish a parser that no
longer exists. Assuming is what T1 forbids. So `resolveWeeklyVolume` returns the
value AND the substitution that produced it, `unitSubstitutions` collapses them
to one entry per token with a row count ("19 rows say `21`" is actionable; 19
identical messages are not), and `combine-project` pushes one warning per token
naming the token, the count, and what it was read as. The population is closed
and shrinking — nothing has been able to add to it since WP 3.2 — so this reports
a set that can only get smaller.

**An ABSENT unit is deliberately NOT reported, and that is the line T1 draws.**
"Absent means weekly" is an explicit default, written into `20260915000001`, the
sidecar and `project_map.py`. T1 permits data, a named substitution rule, or an
explicit default; it forbids the fourth thing, which is a guess. §15 counts 16
rows with a null `time_unit` and they are not a defect — warning about them would
bury the 88 rows that are.

**AND THE HALF THAT WOULD HAVE MADE THE REST DECORATIVE.** `combine-project` has
returned a `warnings` array since WP 0.2, and `DataManager` **discarded it**. The
degradations rode all the way back from the server and stopped one call short of
the only person who could act on them — so "the substitution is always visible at
the point of display" was not met by anything the ETL could have done alone.
`DataManager` now renders each warning, and they do not auto-dismiss: a four-second
toast behind a success message is not visibility. `loudFailure.test.ts` pins both
ends — that the ETL reports the token and does NOT report an absent unit, and that
the page reads `warnings` and shows them with `duration: Infinity`.

`weeklyVolume` keeps its signature, so the arithmetic-only call sites are
untouched and the resolver is strictly additive.
---

#### I · D36 — what closed, what cannot, and why the line is not effort

WP 3.2 closed two paths. This package closed the rest of the ones that CAN be
closed, and the dividing line turned out to be sharper than "six functions, one
line each":

**A write in a transaction the writer controls can be attributed. A PostgREST
call cannot.** A `SECURITY DEFINER` SQL function already runs in a transaction and
can `set_config('app.current_user_id', …, true)` before it writes, so the audit
trigger reads it because it is the same transaction — not because a connection
happened to be reused. An edge function calling PostgREST cannot: the setting
would have to survive into a different statement on a pooled connection, which
`projectLanes.ts`'s own header records that it does not. That is exactly what
D36 meant by "it is NOT a one-line change", and it is why counting lines was
never going to answer it.

**So the SQL writers are closed, including one that was not on the list.**
`assign_material_supplier` writes THREE tier-2/3 tables — `inbound_logistics`,
`supply_chain_data` and `suppliers` — from the /policies grid every time somebody
assigns a supplier to a material. It has taken `p_user_id` since it was written
and never told the trigger, so every one of those writes recorded
`actor_known: false`. It was not among D36's six because nothing had looked at it.
`20260916000021` adds the line; `090` reads the audit row back and asserts it
names the actor, and the mutation that removes the line fires.

That mutation is worth one more sentence, because of HOW it failed. With the line
gone the audit row did not say "unknown" — it named **the user from the previous
assertion block**, whose GUC was still set in the same rehearsal transaction. A
test that only asserted "actor is not null" would have passed. That is the whole
argument for `set_config(…, true)` per transaction rather than per session,
demonstrated by accident.

**The six PostgREST writers are reassigned to WP 4.1, and the reason is
sequencing rather than fatigue.** `combine-project`, `predict-critical-nodes`,
`erp-sync-orbit-mrp` and the three legacy `ingest-*` functions each need their
WRITE moved into an RPC that takes the actor as a parameter. WP 4.1 rewrites how
derived rows are written anyway — that is what `input-hash` is — so those writes
are moving once instead of twice. §11 now says so in the package, and the exit
check is that a rehearsal reads the row back, not that a line was added.

**A limitation of R8, found by conforming to it.** R8's model of a §4 row is
binary: closed (the cell carries ✅) or open (and then it may not name a finished
package). A PARTIAL closure has no representation, so D36's "Closed by" cell
cannot narrate which package closed which half without naming a finished package
and tripping the rule. The cell therefore names the current owner and points at
this section for the history. That is the rule working as designed rather than a
workaround — the column says who owns it NOW, which is the question R8 exists to
keep answerable — but it is recorded because the next partial closure will meet it
too.

---

#### J · A regression this package would have shipped, and did not

A unique index changes what an existing `INSERT` does. Every writer that inserts
into one of the seven tables was re-read for that reason, and one of them breaks:

`ingest-inbound-logistics`, `ingest-outbound-logistics` and
`ingest-bom-multi-level` each did a plain `.insert()`. Before
`20260916000018` a repeated row made a duplicate (D5). After it, the same call
raises **23505** — and `ingest-inbound-logistics` is not dead code: it is the
FALLBACK `StagePolicyTable` uses to assign a supplier to a material when the RPC
path fails. So "assign a supplier who is already assigned" would have gone from
quietly creating a duplicate to failing with a PostgreSQL constraint name in front
of a user who did nothing wrong. Silently duplicating was the defect; failing with
a constraint name is a different defect wearing the fix's clothes.

All three upsert now, on the same key the index enforces. That is a FOURTH place
the key is written down — PostgREST needs the conflict target spelled out — so
`ingestSpecParity.test.ts` checks `onConflict` against `natural_key_intended` too,
and fails if any of them reverts to a bare `.insert()`.

`assign_material_supplier` was checked the same way and is safe: its three
`WHERE NOT EXISTS` guards already make it idempotent. `090` asserts that, because
"I read it and it looked fine" is what a rehearsal exists to replace.

**The general lesson, stated for the next package that adds a constraint:** a
constraint is a change to every existing writer, not only to the table. The list
of writers is findable (`grep` for the table name across `supabase/functions`,
`src/` and the migrations) and checking it is not optional.

---

#### K · §17 was checked by nothing, and now is (R10)

The finding §10 named: §17's sequencing table still said "WP 3.2 is next" after
WP 3.2 shipped. R7 rule 2 gates §16 entries against §7–§13's ✅ markers; nothing
looked at §17 — which is the table a cold session reads FIRST. A status cell no
gate reads is a status cell that decays, and this one decays confidently.

Fixed, and given a rule. **R10** checks the two claims that are unambiguous and
that were both wrong at once:

  1. `"WP N.M is next"` may not name a package §7–§13 marks ✅;
  2. `"N.M ✅"` in §17 may not name a package §7–§13 does not mark ✅ — §17 may
     lag the roadmap, it may never claim more.

It deliberately does not require §17 to mention every done package: a phase row
summarises, and forcing it to enumerate would turn a reader's table into a
changelog. Both halves mutation-tested.

**R10's first run was wrong, and that is recorded rather than tidied away.** It
reported 5.2a and 5.2h as claims §7–§13 does not support. They are supported — the
roadmap marks WP 5.2's sub-packages in a table row (`| **5.2a** ✅ |`) rather than
in a heading, and the rule only read headings. The rule was wrong, not the
document. It reads both forms now, and the comment says why, because a gate that
cries wolf gets relaxed rather than fixed.

**And R8 caught the rest of the same class the moment WP 3.3 was marked ✅**: D5
and D36 both pointed at a package that had just finished. D5 is closed; D36's
remainder moved to WP 4.1 with its reason. That is R8 doing precisely the job the
Phase 2→3 assessment created it for, on its author's own package.
---

#### L · Gap check, baseline numbers, and the handoff

**Exit checks — both, with what proves them rather than the claim.**

| §10's exit check | met | proof |
|---|---|---|
| uploading the same file twice is a no-op | ✅ | `rehearsal/090` §3: two rows after, `rows_updated = 2`, **and the same surrogate ids** — a delete-and-reinsert would satisfy a count and break every reference into the table. Five mutations fire |
| every T2 row traces to a run | ✅ *for rows this path writes* | `ingest_run_id` + `source_row_id` on all nine promotion targets, asserted in `090` §2 including the hop to `source_row_number` — the physical line. **Rows that predate this path carry NULL, and that is the honest state**: a null means the provenance is unknown, never that there was none. Nothing can backfill it, because the files were never stored |

**Baseline numbers:**

**THE HONEST CAVEAT, and it has not changed since WP 3.2 said it.** The dedup

So the distinction to carry forward is sharper than "it is all unproven": the

**The dedup HAS run, and this section originally said it had not.** The
correction is in §16 · B with the numbers; the error is worth its own line here

on merge" is the standing decision about not re-running the workflow BY HAND; it
was read as a description of when the workflow fires, and those are different
claims.

Two consequences, and the second is the one for the next session:

### WP 3.4 — Diff, review, promote UI · 2026-09-17 · `20260917000001`

**Phase 3's last package. Its gap check is therefore a phase handoff, and that
is section L.**

#### A · The handoff, checked against code — three claims held, one did not

§16 · WP 3.3 · L made three checkable claims and the prompt named them. Each was
read against the migration rather than accepted:

| WP 3.3 said | found |
|---|---|
| `ingest_apply_run` is still ONE dynamic statement per target | **TRUE.** One `EXECUTE format('WITH up AS (INSERT … ON CONFLICT … RETURNING)')` per target and nothing else touches tier 2. The second `EXECUTE` in the loop writes tier 1, which carries no audit trigger. The seam is still one statement wide and this package kept it that way: what moved OUT is the fragment-building, not the statement |
| `rows_updated` is computed with `xmax = 0` | **TRUE, and the number is trustworthy for what it counts.** `count(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT inserted)` over `RETURNING (xmax = 0)`. **But it is not what the handoff then said it was** — see B |
| `ingest_run_id` and `source_row_id` are NULL on all 1 691 surviving arcs | **TRUE, and now MEASURED rather than inferred.** §16 · WP 3.3 read it off the absence of runs; §15 had no query for the columns. It has one now: **0 of 6 760 canonical rows across all seven promotion targets carry either** (run `35175080826`) |

**The one that did not hold is the one this package was told to build on.**
WP 3.3's handoff says *"`rows_updated` vs `rows_promoted` is the diff, already
computed … so '12 new, 340 unchanged' needs no second pass over the data."* It is
not the diff. `xmax = 0` separates an INSERT from an UPDATE, and **an UPDATE that
writes identical values is still an UPDATE** — so it cannot distinguish `changed`
from `unchanged`, which is precisely the distinction a person deciding whether to
promote is looking at. "12 new, 340 unchanged" needs a second pass, and §4 D63 is
that finding.

#### B · The central defect, and it was not recorded anywhere (D62)

`ingest_staged_rows.diff_state` is `NOT NULL DEFAULT 'new'`, CHECK-constrained to
four tokens — and **`20260916000019` does not contain the string once.** Nothing
has ever written it. So every CSV row ever staged claims `new`, including the rows
the upsert UPDATED.

**A default that is present and wrong is worse than a null**, and the sidecar had
already reasoned its way into defending it: *"every CSV row says `new` because that
is what an uncompared row is."* That sentence is the defect in prose. An uncompared
row is not new; it is uncompared. A review screen reading the column today renders
"340 new" for 340 unchanged rows — confidently, with a number, from a column nobody
computed.

The DEFAULT and the NOT NULL are both dropped and existing rows set to NULL. They
had to go together: NOT NULL with no default cannot be inserted by
`ingest_land_file`, and NOT NULL with a default is the defect. The three CONNECTOR
staging tables keep theirs and that is not an inconsistency —
`erp-sync-orbit-mrp` computes and writes `diff_state` on every row it stages, so
the default is never the value that survives. **This column's default was
load-bearing precisely because nothing wrote it.**

**Its twin, and a third with the same cause.** `ingest_apply_run` set
`rows_new = v_total`, where `v_total` is inserts AND updates, and never wrote
`rows_changed` or `rows_unchanged` (D63); and it wrote the count of rows HELD BACK
into `rows_removed`, whose sidecar says it means `removed_upstream` (D64). Three
columns the review screen reads: one holding a number that is not what it is named,
two holding zeroes that are not measurements, and a fourth holding an unrelated
fact. All three are the same shape — **the function knew the answer, returned it,
and had nowhere to put it.** `rows_held` and `rows_superseded` are columns now.

#### C · Where the diff is computed, which is the design §10's line hides

§10 says "compute `diff_state`". It does not say when, and when is the whole
design. A `diff_state` written by `ingest_apply_run` is written AFTER the decision
it exists to inform: the review screen shows the diff so a person can decide
whether to promote, and a diff that only exists once the rows are in tier 2 answers
a question nobody is still asking.

So `ingest_diff_run` compares against the CURRENT tier-2 rows, and runs **three
times**: at landing, again when the review screen asks, and again inside
`ingest_apply_run` in the same transaction as the upsert. The third is what makes
the number honest — tier 2 can change between the review and the click, and a
promotion reporting the review's answer would be reporting a number it already
knew to be stale.

**Nothing is restated.** The natural key comes from `ingest_target_natural_key()`
(WP 3.3, read from `pg_index`), and the written columns and their normalized values
come from **`ingest_promotion_plan()`, which was lifted OUT of `ingest_apply_run`**
rather than copied. `ingestSpecParity.test.ts` already pins three copies of the
keys; a fourth was the alternative and this is why there is not one. The promotion's
statement is unchanged — it now reads its fragments instead of building them.

**Three details that are not decoration:**

  - **The key predicate joins with `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM`, not `=`.** Three of the
    seven natural keys contain a nullable column whose NULL is meaningful, so every
    index is `NULLS NOT DISTINCT` and `ON CONFLICT` treats two NULLs as the same
    key (D5). A diff joining with `=` finds no match for exactly those rows, calls
    them `new`, and then watches the upsert UPDATE them — the review screen and the
    promotion disagreeing about the same row, in the one case no constraint had
    ever covered before WP 3.3. `rehearsal/100` §6 uploads a BOM root twice.
  - **The comparison runs AFTER normalization**, against the value that would
    actually land. Comparing the raw cell would report a change every time a file
    restated 7/week as 30.4375/month, which is the same fact twice. `100` §5
    restates an arc in days — 2 a day is 14 a week, 14 days is 2 weeks, and they
    are not inverses — and requires `unchanged`.
  - **The superseded finding MOVED here from the promotion.** WP 3.3 wrote it as a
    side effect of applying; the review screen shows the third row state, so it has
    to exist before the decision. Its wording is present-tense so the same sentence
    is true at review time and afterwards, and the diff strips any previous copy
    before recomputing — three callers means a row is diffed repeatedly, and a
    second pass that appended would inflate `rows_superseded` on every refresh.

**`removed_upstream`, decided in writing because §10 asked.** It is in the CHECK
vocabulary and this function never writes it. A connector PULL is a statement about
the whole source — the row is gone from the system of record. A FILE is not that
statement: nothing about `inbound-january.csv` says it is the complete set of a
project's lanes, and a user uploading one plant's arcs would otherwise be told their
other plants had been removed upstream. So `rows_removed` is 0 for every file run,
and the screen prints *"an upload cannot remove rows: a file is not a statement
about the rows it omits"* instead of the zero. §5 T1 has no fourth option, and that
includes a zero.

#### D · D61 — the precondition nobody had hit, because nobody had called the resolver

§10's exit check is "promotion by an analyst is REFUSED", and the function to read
is `effective_project_role`, which has existed since WP 2.2. Landing the gate on it
exposed something underneath: **`project_members` has had exactly one writer in its
life and it ran once**, inside `20260915000005` — "every project's modeler becomes
its owner", which is the right rule, applied to the rows that existed that day and
never again. No trigger, no RPC, no application code inserts a member.

So every project created after 2026-09-15 has no members, its own creator resolves
to a NULL role, and `project_role_rank(NULL)` is 0 — below `viewer`. **A role gate
landed on top of that is not a gate, it is an outage**: it would have refused the
promotion of every file in every new project, including by the person who created
it.

It was invisible because `subtractive-delegation` (G3) is gated source-level only
and **no live code path had ever called the resolver.** WP 3.4 is the first, which
is the general lesson: a governance function nothing calls is a governance function
nothing tests, and the first caller pays for every year of that.

Closed with the writer WP 2.2's rule needed — `project_owner_membership()` on an
`AFTER INSERT` trigger, plus the same backfill re-run `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` so it
never demotes a member since given a smaller role on purpose.

**And §15 says it was latent, not yet damaging**: 10 projects, 9 memberships, **0
projects whose modeler is not a member.** No project has been created since WP 2.2
deployed. The defect was one project-creation away, which is the difference between
finding it now and finding it in a support ticket.

#### E · The role gate replaces `has_project_access`; it does not join it

`ingest_apply_run` checked `has_project_access` — "the modeler, or a platform
admin" — and never a role (D65). It now checks `project_role_rank(...) >= rank
('editor')` and **the access check is gone**, for two reasons that point the same
way. Two authorities for one question is `single-source` (I1) broken inside the
governance plane. And keeping both would have refused an EDITOR who is not the
project's modeler, which is the entire point of having editors.

**What that tightens, said plainly rather than discovered later:** a platform
`admin` who is neither the modeler nor a member can no longer promote into a
project. `has_project_access` admitted them; the role model does not. A
`super_admin` still can — `effective_project_role` resolves them to `owner`. This
is a deliberate narrowing and the remedy is a membership row, not a second branch.

**The exit check is a statement about the DATABASE.** A disabled button is not a
refusal: the RPC is reachable without the bundle that draws the button.
`rehearsal/100` §3 promotes as an analyst who is a genuine member and requires
`insufficient_privilege`, that the run stays `staged`, and that tier 2 is untouched.
The screen's button reads its enabled state from the same function — returned by
`ingest_diff_run` as `actor_may_promote` — so it PREVIEWS the refusal and is never
a substitute for it.

#### F · What the rehearsal found that no static gate could (D31, twice more)

**`rehearsal/100`'s first run failed inside `ingest_apply_run`**, and the failure is
D66. The editor passed the role gate and was then refused by `ingest_diff_run`'s
`has_project_access` check — because the RLS on every ingest table routes through
that predicate while the promotion now reads a rank. **`min_project_role` is
declared on all 37 tables in the contract and read by nothing** (`declared-capability`
is gated by the block EXISTING), so the system has two live answers to "may this
person touch this project" and they disagree for exactly the person §10 says may
promote. Found by an assertion, not by review. The read gate is the UNION of the two
today and the comment says why: that is the honest shape of a half-migrated
governance plane, not belt and braces. WP 6.2 owns moving RLS onto the resolver.

**And one mutation exposed a bug in the test rather than in the code.** Disabling
the D61 trigger left `rehearsal/100` GREEN: the assertion was
`IF effective_project_role(...) <> 'owner'`, and the function returns NULL for a
non-member, and `NULL <> 'owner'` is NULL, which an `IF` treats as false. **The
assertion guarding the precondition could never fail.** It is `IS DISTINCT FROM`
now, and so is every other text comparison in the file. A test that cannot fail is
the exact failure mode this plan exists to end, and it was found by mutating — not
by reading it twice.

Eight mutations run against `100`, every one fired with its own message:

| mutation | what fired |
|---|---|
| `diff_state` keeps its `NOT NULL DEFAULT 'new'` | "4 staged row(s) carry a diff_state before anything computed one" |
| the diff joins the natural key with `=` | "re-uploading a BOM ROOT — whose natural key contains a NULL — diffed as new=1" |
| the role gate removed | "an ANALYST promoted a run" |
| the comparison reads the raw cell, not the normalized value | "one identical, one edited and one unseen row diffed as new=1 changed=2" |
| a re-diff does not strip its previous findings | "re-running the diff left 2 superseded finding(s), expected 1" |
| `rows_new = v_total` restored | "after the second promotion the run holds new=3 changed=0 unchanged=0" |
| the held count back in `rows_removed` | "a file run reported rows_removed=1" |
| the membership trigger disabled | "a project created now gives its modeler the role \"(none)\"" |

Four more were run against the TypeScript suite — a `source_kind` branch in the
component, the role gate deleted from the SQL, the landing promoting again, and a
null `diff_state` rendering as "new" — and all four fired.

#### G · One component, both sources — §10's gap check, and how it is held

**There is no branch on `source_kind` beyond labels.** `IngestRunReview` reads it
twice, both through a lookup: `sourceLabel()` and `removalNote()`, the second being
a sentence chosen per source, which is a label with more words and is named as the
exemption rather than left to look accidental.

A claim about ABSENCE decays the first time somebody adds a convenience, so
`ingestDiffReview.test.ts` counts the occurrences and requires them all to go
through the two functions — **with comments stripped first**, because this codebase
explains its rules at length and a test that counted the explanation would fail for
the wrong reason. It also checks the label table covers exactly the `source_kind`
CHECK's vocabulary, and that the diff vocabulary in TypeScript is the `diff_state`
CHECK's token for token: a screen rendering a fifth state the database cannot store
is a screen with a category that will always be empty.

**`MappingWarningsCard`'s `WARN_META` is now EXPORTED and imported.** §10 said
"reuse its badge vocabulary rather than inventing a second", and a vocabulary you
cannot import is a vocabulary you copy. The test fails if the review screen declares
its own.

**Three row states, not two.** WP 3.3's handoff was right that there are three, and
they are rendered as three: promoted, held back with the error that held it, and
superseded-by-a-later-line with the finding naming the line that won. An error
outranks a supersession, so a held row is never shown as promoted.

**And the screen states the limit of its own comparison** (§5 T3). When the five
counts do not account for every staged row it says so, in words, instead of showing
five numbers that quietly lose rows.

#### H · The click-through is a join, and the NULL case is 100 % of production

tier-2 row → `source_row_id` → `ingest_staged_rows.source_row_number` (the physical
line, header = line 1) → `ingest_run_id` → `ingest_files` (filename,
`content_sha256`). `rehearsal/100` §7 asserts all four hops as one query and requires
the line number to be 3, which is where that arc was in the file.

`RowProvenance` renders it, on the item-master grid (the item masters became
promotion targets in WP 3.3, D55) and in the review screen. **It resolves the hops
as separate reads on purpose**: both FK columns are `ON DELETE SET NULL`, so a
staged row that outlived its file still yields the LINE, and a line is most of what
a person wanted.

**A NULL is UNKNOWN, never "there was none", and today it is every row.** §15 run
`35175080826`: **0 of 6 760** rows across the seven promotion targets carry either
column. Rendering "no source" for those would be a false statement about 100 % of
the data; rendering nothing would be §5 T1's fourth option. It says *"source
unknown — this row was written before uploads were traced, or the run that wrote it
has since been deleted; it is not a row that came from nowhere."*

#### I · D28 had no owner, and the gate built to catch that could not see it

§4 D28's "Closed by" cell read `Phase 3`, on the strength of its own text — closing
it "needs an auth model, which is a Phase 3 package". **No such package was ever
written.** The moment this package ships, D28 is a defect owned by a FINISHED PHASE,
which is D41 exactly, standing in the blind spot of R8 — the rule built to prevent
D41 — because R8's regex matches `WP N.M` and `Phase 3` does not match.

Three changes, in one commit:

  1. **R8 reads phase-level owners.** A phase is finished when every package the
     roadmap lists for it is ✅, derived from the same markers rather than from
     §17's prose so the two cannot disagree. It fires only when the cell names NO
     package at all — D36's cell cites "§16 · Phase 3's last package" and is owned
     by WP 4.1, and reading that as a second owner is the gate crying wolf, which
     gets it relaxed rather than fixed.
  2. **R8 refuses an owner the plan does not contain.** A typo'd or invented
     package is the same failure arriving by a different door. **Its first run
     found D21 pointing at WP 5.2b** — which was the RULE being wrong: sub-packages
     of WP 5.2 live in a table, not in a heading, exactly as R10 had to learn.
  3. **§14 gains `WP 7.1 — the authentication model`**, so D28 has an owner that
     exists. It is DEFERRED, not scheduled, and the standing decision is unchanged:
     document, do not change. What the package is, when it runs, is written out —
     sessions the database can read, `auth.uid()` in place of the GUC, the 27
     predicate-less policies made RESTRICTIVE, `anon`'s 14 write grants revoked, and
     D36 closed for good, because an actor read from a verified token is
     attribution where a client-asserted id checked against `has_project_access` is
     only a constraint.

R8 now reports `16 done, 4 finished phase(s), 35 named`.

#### J · §15, and the fourth run lost to the same race through a third door

**Before** (run `35172930134`, 2026-09-17, before any migration in this package):

| | all projects |
|---|---|
| `inbound_logistics` / `outbound` / `bom_single` / `bom_multi` | **1 691** (7 projects) / **38** (7) / **2 907** (5) / **792** (2) |
| rows a unique index would reject, all seven targets | **0** — WP 3.3's dedup holds |

| connector: runs · staged_products · links | **0 · 0 · 0** |

**THE AFTER-RUN WAS LOST, AND THE DOOR IS NEW.** Run `35175080826` fired on the
migration push and its own report carries the proof: *`column r.rows_superseded
does not exist`*. It did not touch `.github/verify-request`. **It edited

path**, alongside the request file and the workflow itself — and this package added
four probes to that runner in the same commit as the migration.

§16 · WP 3.3 · L's rule says "push the migration, wait for the deploy, THEN touch
`.github/verify-request`". That names one of three doors. **Fourth run lost in three
packages, and the first through a door the rule did not name.** The rule is widened
in CLAUDE.md: *a push that carries a migration must change none of the three.*

The raced report is not worthless — its two pre-migration reads are genuine
before-numbers and are used above: **0 of 6 760 canonical rows carry provenance**,
and **10 projects / 9 memberships / 0 modelers who are not members**.

**After** — see section K.

#### K · §15, after — and the delta is deliberately almost nothing

Run `35175348248`, 2026-09-17, taken after `Deploy Supabase Migrations` reported

**Almost nothing moved, and that is the correct result for this package.** Every

**One defect in a probe this package wrote, found by the report rather than by the

#### L · Gap check, exit checks, and the PHASE 3 → 4 HANDOFF

**§10's exit checks — all three met, with the proof rather than the claim.**

| exit check | met | proof |
|---|---|---|
| a user can click from a cell through to the source row | ✅ | `rehearsal/100` §7 asserts the four hops as one query and requires line **3**, which is where that arc sat in the file. `RowProvenance` renders it on the item-master grid and in the review screen; a NULL says "source unknown" and why |
| promotion by an analyst is refused | ✅ | `rehearsal/100` §3, against a real database, with an analyst who is a genuine member. Mutation-tested. The run stays `staged` and tier 2 is untouched — a gate that half-applied would be worse than none |
| **one** component serves both CSV and MRP runs | ✅ | two reads of `source_kind`, both through a lookup, counted by `ingestDiffReview.test.ts` with comments stripped |

**Gap check — §10's own question.** *Any branch on `source_kind` beyond labels
means WP 3.1 was incomplete.* **There is none**, and WP 3.1 is vindicated: the diff,
the promotion, the hook and the screen are all written against a run, not against a
source. What one costs is a two-entry label table and one sentence.

**Baseline numbers:**
  - **294 tests**, 265 → 294. `ingestDiffReview.test.ts` is new (29).
  - **Nine rehearsal files**, green **all three ways** before every push — including
    `--since HEAD`, against the artifact this branch WROTE, which is the mode the
    WP 3.1 follow-up added after `main` went red on a dangling foreign key (D52).
    The introspector followed the new function and the new trigger correctly: 245 →
    248 functions in the third-mode base.
  - **Twelve mutations** run — eight against `rehearsal/100`, four against the
    TypeScript suite — every one fired with its own message, and one of them found a

  - `contract:check` green with **zero warnings**. R1 unchanged at 37/42/79 — this
    package described no new table. R8 now reports `16 done, 4 finished phase(s), 35
    named`.
  - `check:docs` green.

**What is red on `main` and is not this package's.** `npm run lint` (453 problems
repo-wide), `scsim engine tests` (the `browser-wheels` job — the committed wheel

**THE HONEST CAVEAT, and it has not changed since WP 3.2 first wrote it.** The CSV
path has still run **zero** times in production: `csv_runs 0 · staged_rows 0 ·
csv_files 0 · landing_audit_rows 0`, measured after this package's own migration
deployed. So every screen built here renders data that has only ever existed in
`supabase/rehearsal/070`, `080`, `090` and `100`. The MRP side is emptier still —
the connector has never been used at all, so "one component, both sources" is

**A green rehearsal is not a working pipeline.** The first production upload is the
real test of WP 3.2 and 3.3; the first one somebody REVIEWS and then promotes is the
test of this package, and the first one they decline to promote is the test of the
part nothing can rehearse — whether the diff told them something they could act on.

---

### WP 4.1 — Complete and compose `graph_hash` · 2026-09-17 · `20260917000002`–`20260917000005`

#### A · The failing test, and it is the whole of D11 in one message

On `main`, on a multi-level project, this happens:

```
UPDATE bom_multi_level SET consumption_rate = 4 WHERE material_id = 'M1';
  → current_graph_hash: 41fe51ca7963  (unchanged)
  → snapshot_dataset:   the SAME version id
```

`supabase/rehearsal/110` §1 was written to fail on exactly that, before the fix,
against a real PostgreSQL 16, and its message says why rather than that:
`datamap.py:214-219` reads `bom_multi_level` FIRST and falls back to
`bom_single_level` only when the deep table is empty. So on a multi-level project
v1 hashed the one BOM table the run did **not** read. 792 rows across two
production projects sit in that table today.

**The rule is the defect, and the table was one symptom.** v1's own header says
"Column sets mirror `datamap.py` exactly", which requires a person to re-mirror a
Python file whenever the engine changes. Writing the comparison down as code
found two more it had already missed (**D67**):

  - `lead_time_unit` — the engine PROJECTS it, with a comment naming D9, because
    PostgREST returns only what the projection names. v1 hashed `lead_time`
    without it, so **14 days and 14 weeks were the same dataset**.
  - `demand_min` / `demand_max` — added to `products` after v1, read by
    `build_project_data`, never hashed.

And a third defect that no amount of mirroring would have caught (**D68**):
`jsonb_agg(... ORDER BY ...)` fixes an order only as far as the ORDER BY
discriminates, and v1's orderings were not total — `inbound` ordered by
`supplier_id, material_id, unit_price, volume` with no `plant_name`, so two rows
in different plants that tie on all four come back in an unspecified order and
produce two different hashes from one dataset. WP 3.3's unique indexes make that
impossible *within* a plant and do nothing across plants. **A hash that is not a
function of its input is not an identity**, and it fails silently in both
directions: dirty when nothing changed, or two runs on identical data reported as
different worlds.

#### B · v2's rule, and the gate that is the actual deliverable

> **The snapshot hashes every VALUE column of every tier-2 INPUT table** — every
> column except the surrogate `id`, the `project_id` it is already scoped to, the
> audit timestamps, the ingestion provenance and the cosmetic `name`.

Mechanical, checkable, and it does not need anybody to notice. `graphHashCoverage.test.ts`
reads the generated contract, `datamap.py` and the migration, and fails when a
tier-2 value column or an engine-projected column is absent from the snapshot. It
also asserts the parse found something at all — a scan that silently finds nothing
is a green test that checks nothing, which is this plan's recurring failure mode.

Every `ORDER BY` is now the table's UNIQUE natural key (WP 3.3's, read from
`pg_index` by `ingest_target_natural_key` in the sibling RPC), so the ordering is
total by construction. D68 is the one defect here whose fix was cheaper than the
defect: nothing to add, only the right columns to order by.

**The cost of the new rule, named rather than discovered later:** it produces a
CONSERVATIVE DIRTY. Renaming a plant moves the hash although no run reads
`plant_name`. That is the safe direction for a trust anchor — a false "changed" is
visible and a missed one is not (§5 T2) — and it is a real cost that somebody will
report as a bug.

**`customers` is hashed although nothing reads it, and asking why turned up D69.**
`project_map.py:574` synthesizes `Customer(id=c, name=c)` from the ids in
`outbound_logistics` and never loads the `customers` table — while `scsim`'s P-C.2
reads `Customer.priority_weight` and `Customer.segment` to decide who gets served
when supply is short. So a user who fills in a customer's priority changes nothing,
silently, on every project. Six rows across five production projects carry values.
Hashing the columns now means the day that reader lands the anchor already covers
them; the alternative is a second `schema_version` bump, and section C is what one
of those costs.

#### C · THE DECISION THIS PACKAGE HAD TO MAKE, AND THE NUMBERS IT WAS MADE AGAINST

**Decision: bump `schema_version` 1 → 2, in one step, including the columns beyond
D11's literal text.** Written down here because §11 says a bump is not local and
the thing that bites is never the change, it is the reader nobody enumerated.

The brief said `current_graph_hash` "has four live readers". It has **eighteen call
sites across sixteen files**, and the one that matters was described as "does more
than display", which undersells it. `expire_agent_proposals` does not mark a
proposal invalid — it **UPDATEs `proposals.status` to `expired` with
`status_reason = 'grounding_drift'`**, for every row in `draft`, `proposed` or
**`approved`**, and `list_agent_proposals` calls it, so the write happens on the
first page load after the deploy. The predicate is one-way: nothing un-expires a
proposal when the hash comes back. That is a persisted, irreversible status
transition triggered by a READ, and no document in this repository said so. **D70.**

So §15 was run BEFORE the migration, in its own push, to turn the fear into a
count. What it found:

| what the bump touches | before | consequence |
|---|---|---|
| `proposals` live and grounded on a `graph_hash` | **0** (1 proposal exists, 0 live) | **nothing is expired** |
| `model_validations` active cards | **0** | nothing stales |
| `project_memory` rows grounded on a hash | **0** | nothing stales |
| `dataset_versions` | 6, across 4 of 10 projects | all 6 immutable and untouched; the next freeze inserts rather than dedups |
| `simulation_runs` | 17, **17 bound to a version, 0 whose version is gone** | §11's second exit check, measured |

**So the bump is free, and the reason it is free is that nobody has used those
features yet — not that the mechanism is safe.** On any day
`live_grounded_on_graph_hash` is not zero, the same deploy expires them one-way
with no undo. The mitigation is now permanent: §15 counts it before every bump,
and the rule that a hash change is a reversible display state and never a persisted
status write is WP 4.4's to land (D70).

**What DOES change on the day it deploys:** the 4 projects that have ever been
frozen read dirty until somebody freezes again, and all 17 completed runs read
dirty against their project. For the two multi-level projects that is not a
regression — those runs were dirty all along and v1's hash could not say so.

#### D · D36, closed for all six, and the three things that move with it

Four RPCs in `20260917000003`, each taking the actor as a PARAMETER through one
shared preamble (`assert_writer_may_act`) that refuses a NULL actor and sets
`app.current_user_id` LOCAL:

| edge function | RPC | what it wrote before |
|---|---|---|
| `ingest-inbound-logistics`, `ingest-outbound-logistics`, `ingest-bom-multi-level` | `ingest_legacy_upsert_lane` | a tier-2 lane, direct `.upsert()`, key spelled in TypeScript |
| `erp-sync-orbit-mrp` | `mrp_apply_staged_products` | `products`, ONE ROW AT A TIME |
| `combine-project` | `etl_replace_supply_chain` | DELETE then INSERT on two tier-3 tables, separate calls |
| `predict-critical-nodes` | `analysis_mark_critical_nodes` | one UPDATE PER PREDICTION |

**Three things move that are not the audit, and they are why this is worth more
than an `actor_user_id` column:**

  1. **`no-tier-skip` (I2) stops being a property of three files.** The handoff
     records that the invariant holds for the nine CSV datasets "by the ABSENCE of
     any other write path, which is a property of today's code and not a check".
     While those three functions held a PostgREST client they were one `.upsert()`
     away from any tier-2 table in the schema. The set they can now reach is a
     whitelist in a migration, checked before it reaches `format()` — a dynamic
     INSERT whose table name came from a caller is an injection with a migration
     around it.
  2. **`erp-sync-orbit-mrp` was a SECOND PROMOTION PATH and nothing had said so.**
     `applyStagedRun` read `ingest_staged_products` and upserted `products` — a
     tier-1 → tier-2 promotion that never went through `ingest_apply_run` and
     carried no actor. The handoff's "all NINE CSV datasets" was true and this is
     not a CSV dataset. It still answers to no project ROLE, and that is now a
     stated decision rather than an oversight — see below.
  3. **The audit log stops being unreadable.** §15's before-run measured **2 575**
     `supply_chain_data` UPDATE rows with `actor_known: false` out of 2 580
     data-plane rows in the whole database. That is `predict-critical-nodes`'s
     per-row loop, in the log WP 2.3 chose the statement grain to keep readable.
     One statement now, one row.

**The RPCs AUTHENTICATE and do not AUTHORIZE, and that is a decision reversed
mid-package.** `20260917000003` refused below project role `editor`; it seemed like
free hardening and it was a live narrowing. `effective_project_role` grants `owner`
to a SUPER admin and to nobody else by role — `is_super_admin` reads
`role = 'super_admin'` — so an ORGANIZATION admin who is not a project member
resolves to NULL, below `viewer`. `combine-project` has always permitted exactly
that user (`modeler_id = user_id OR role = 'admin'`), so the gate would have refused
the ETL from the DataManager button, silently, as an `insufficient_privilege` from a
function the user has never heard of.

Three things said it should come out and none of them is taste. §11 asks for no such
check. The one precedent for this exact class of fix — `assign_material_supplier`,
the sibling /policies writer WP 3.3 closed for D36 — sets the GUC and checks no role.
And `ingest_apply_run`'s gate is not a counter-example: §10 asked for it in as many
words, and WP 3.4 REPLACED `has_project_access` with it rather than adding a second
authority, "because two authorities for one question is `single-source` broken in
the governance plane". Adding one on TOP of each function's existing authorization is
the second authority WP 3.4 declined to create.

`20260917000005` takes it out. Each caller keeps the authorization it already had.
**That is not a claim that the current authorization is right — it is D66**, and an
ad-hoc partial enforcement on four RPCs would have been one more divergence in the
plane whose divergences WP 6.2 exists to close. `rehearsal/110` §7a now pins the
ABSENCE: an analyst is accepted, deliberately, and the mutation that re-adds the gate
turns the file red with a message pointing at the migration that removed it — so the
next reader meets a decision rather than a hole they think they are closing.

**And auto-apply had to be given a real actor rather than a blank.** The scheduled
path passed `null`; the RPC refuses a NULL actor outright, so "who is a scheduled
sync" had to be answered. It is `project_erp_links.linked_by_user_id` — the person
who created the link and set the threshold authorized this write when they
configured it. **That is attribution to whoever authorized the automation, not to a
person present at the time**, and the two are different claims; `triggered_by`
already records which kind of run it was. If that person no longer holds `editor`
the refusal is caught and the run is left `staged` for a human, which is the right
outcome and not a failed sync.

#### E · THE ASSERTION THAT PASSED FOR THE WRONG REASON, found by a mutation

Section 7 of `rehearsal/110` performs each write and SELECTs the audit row back,
as §11 requires. The first draft asserted the row named `v_owner`. It was green.
So was the mutation that **deleted `set_config` from `assert_writer_may_act`
entirely**.

The whole file is one `DO` block, therefore one transaction, and
`set_config(..., true)` is transaction-LOCAL — so `snapshot_dataset`, asserted two
sections earlier, had already put `v_owner` in the GUC and left it there. Every
"the RPC names its actor" assertion was reading a value a previous statement had
set.

It now POISONS the GUC with `v_analyst` immediately before each call and makes the
write as `v_editor`, so a row naming `v_editor` can only have come from the RPC
setting it. Both GUC mutations fire, and the message names the poisoned user so the
next reader sees the mechanism rather than a mismatch.

**This is WP 3.4's finding arriving again in a new costume** (§16 · WP 3.4 · F
found `NULL <> 'owner'` in an assertion). Twice now the bug has been in the test.
The rule that catches it is not "be careful": it is *run the mutation, and when it
does not fire, the test is what is wrong.*

**Nineteen mutations, every one red with its own message.** Six against the
snapshot (drop `bom_multi_level`, drop `lead_time_unit`, drop `demand_min`/`max`,
drop `customers`, hash the whole text instead of the domains, digest the whole
snapshot as `hash_network`), two against the GUC (remove it; keep whatever the
connection already held), seven against the RPCs (remove the role check while it still existed, remove the
NULL-actor check, disable the target whitelist, promote `removed_upstream` rows,
accept a cross-project score set, remove the GUC from the actor-only preamble, and
RE-ADD the role gate the decision removed), and two against the ratchet (a 27th
unattributed writer; `snapshot_dataset` losing its GUC).

#### F · D71 — D36 WAS ONE SLICE OF A CLASS, AND THE CLASS IS 26

D36 counted the service-role PostgREST writers, because that is where WP 2.3
looked. WP 3.3 then found `assign_material_supplier` — a `SECURITY DEFINER` SQL
function that had taken the actor as a parameter all along and never told the
trigger — and D36's own evidence says it "was never in the list of six because
nothing had looked at it". This package found a second the same way:
**`snapshot_dataset` has recorded `actor_known: false` on every dataset version
ever frozen, beside an `author_user_id` the caller supplied.**

Two instances found by accident is a class, so the gap check measured it:

```
26  SECURITY DEFINER functions write a tier-2/3/4 table
 2  set app.current_user_id   (assign_material_supplier, snapshot_dataset)
16  of the remaining 24 already TAKE an actor parameter
17  have at least one live caller in src/ or supabase/functions/
```

Every one is the one-line fix D36 correctly says is NOT one for a PostgREST call,
because a `SECURITY DEFINER` function runs in a transaction it controls.

**So the honest statement is that `audit-actor` (G4) is NOT met after this package**,
and closing D36 must not be reported as though it were. CLAUDE.md's row says so.

A gate would be red on arrival and therefore unlandable, so what shipped is a
RATCHET: `dataPlaneAudit.test.ts` holds the measured list and fails when a 27th
appears **and** when a name that is now attributed is left on it, so the number can
shrink and cannot grow. Mutation-tested both ways. Three of the listed names do set
the GUC, through the shared preamble, and they stay on the list because a text scan
cannot follow a call — quietly special-casing them would make the ratchet lie about
its own method, and the rehearsal is what proves those three.

#### G · What the parity gate did when the key moved, which is the right thing

`ingestSpecParity.test.ts` went RED on this branch: it asserts the three legacy
functions name `onConflict` matching the sidecar's `natural_key_intended`, and they
no longer name a key at all — `ingest_legacy_upsert_lane` reads the arbiter from
`pg_index`. The fourth copy of the key is gone.

The test gets STRONGER rather than being relaxed. It now asserts the three name no
key, no conflict target and no tier-2 table by any PostgREST verb, and that each
passes an actor; a second block holds D36's other three to the same rule. A future
edit that puts `.from('supply_chain_data').insert(...)` back is `no-tier-skip` and
`audit-actor` failing together, silently, in a file nobody is looking at.

**`min(uuid)` does not exist in PostgreSQL**, and the first draft of
`analysis_mark_critical_nodes` used it. The rehearsal said so; nothing static would
have. That is the third package running in which the rehearsal found a defect in
the migration rather than in the schema.

#### G2 · A correction to an APPLIED migration is a new migration, not an edit

Caught between the deploy and the after-run, and worth a paragraph because the
near-miss is silent by construction.

`ingest_legacy_upsert_lane` built its quoted column list and then SPLIT IT BACK
on `', '` to derive the value list and the `DO UPDATE SET` fragment — a fact it
already held, re-derived from a weaker source, and a split that would mis-parse
any identifier needing a quoted spelling. The fix was written as an edit to
`20260917000003` and reverted, because by then `supabase-migrations.yml` had
already deployed it (§4 D31: no branch filter, so a branch push deploys).
**Supabase tracks applied migrations by version, so re-pushing an edited
`20260917000003` would have been SKIPPED** — leaving the file and production
disagreeing about what the function contains, with nothing in the repository
able to notice. The schema probe compares TABLES, `contract:rehearse` runs the
file rather than production, and an artifact generated from the edited file
would have agreed with the file and been wrong about the database.

It is `20260917000004` instead, which says so in its own header. Note what did
NOT catch this: `rehearsal/110` §7a passes identically either way, because the
two derivations produce the same statement. It needed reading.

#### H · Two shapes of `snapshot` live forever, and the export had to learn both

A frozen version is IMMUTABLE — that is what lets a run resolve the dataset it
actually ran against — so every v1 row keeps the v1 shape (six tables at the top
level) while v2 nests them under `inputs` and adds `network`. A reader that handles
only the new one exports empty sheets for every historical version, silently.
`verifiableExports.ts` reads both, and `_meta` states which it is looking at.

The v1 caveat gets sharper rather than disappearing. A v1 workbook now carries a
**Known limit** row saying its `graph_hash` does not cover `bom_multi_level`,
`lead_time_unit`, `demand_min`/`demand_max`, `customers` or the network tables, and
— when the deep-BOM sheet is present — that those rows were read LIVE and are not
part of what the hash covers, so they may have changed since the freeze. Nothing
can repair that after the fact; saying so is the whole of §5 T3. From v2 the deep
BOM comes out of the snapshot and the caveat is gone with it, replaced by the one
that is still true: the four DERIVED network tables are not in the hash and WP 4.2
binds them to their own.

`useDatasetVersion` gains `dirtyDomain`, and the distinction is not cosmetic:
`inputs` dirty means a completed run cannot be reproduced, `network` dirty means a
multi-tier analysis is stale and no simulation changed. Telling a user to re-run
everything because a deep-tier upload landed would be a false alarm. It returns
`null` for a project whose latest version predates this migration — those rows have
no domain hashes and nothing can backfill them, and **`null` there means UNKNOWN,
not "nothing moved"**.

#### I · GAP CHECK — every tier-2 table against the snapshot

§11 asks for this table by name, because a missing row is a silent blind spot of
exactly the kind this package exists to close. Tiers are the contract's own, and
the four DERIVED tables are included although they are not in the contract —
leaving them out is how a blind spot stays one.

| table | tier | in `graph_hash`? | why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `suppliers` | 2 | ✅ `hash_inputs` | engine input |
| `materials` | 2 | ✅ `hash_inputs` | engine input |
| `products` | 2 | ✅ `hash_inputs` | engine input; `demand_min`/`demand_max` added here (D67) |
| `customers` | 2 | ✅ `hash_inputs` | an INPUT a user typed. **No reader loads it today** (D69) — hashed so the anchor already covers it when one does |
| `inbound_logistics` | 2 | ✅ `hash_inputs` | engine input; `lead_time_unit` added here (D67) |
| `outbound_logistics` | 2 | ✅ `hash_inputs` | engine input |
| `bom_single_level` | 2 | ✅ `hash_inputs` | engine input — the fallback when the deep table is empty |
| `bom_multi_level` | 2 | ✅ `hash_inputs` | engine input, and the one it PREFERS (D11) |
| `tier2_suppliers` | 2 | ✅ `hash_network` | deep-tier input. **0 rows in production** |
| `tier3_suppliers` | 2 | ✅ `hash_network` | deep-tier input. **0 rows in production** |
| `multi_tier_supply_chain` | 2 | ✅ `hash_network` | deep-tier input. **0 rows in production** |
| `supply_chain_data` | 3 | ❌ deliberately | DERIVED — `combine-project`'s ETL output. A tier-3 row is a function of tier 2; hashing it would move the anchor when nothing a user typed changed. WP 4.3 gives it `computed_from_hash` |
| `supply_chain_data_multi_tier` | 3 | ❌ deliberately | same, same owner |
| `dataset_versions` | 3 | ❌ by construction | it IS the hash's home; hashing it would be circular |
| `policy_defaults` | 4 | ❌ deliberately | the POLICY plane, bound by `policy_hash`. A run binds dataset **and** policy separately and must (I8) |
| `policy_overrides` | 4 | ❌ deliberately | same. WP 4.4 adds `seeded_from_hash` so a re-upload can flag a stale seeded override |
| `risk_data` | reference | ❌ deliberately | a property of the WORLD, not of a project — no `project_id`, and a country's risk class changing is not a change to anybody's dataset |
| `node_list` | *deferred* | ❌ **WP 4.2** | DERIVED — an analysis wrote it |
| `network_nodes` | *deferred* | ❌ **WP 4.2** | DERIVED — centralities written by `calculate-network-science-metrics` |
| `network_edges` | *deferred* | ❌ **WP 4.2** | DERIVED |
| `network_summary` | *deferred* | ❌ **WP 4.2** | DERIVED — a roll-up of the two above |

**No tier-2 table is unaccounted for**, and `graphHashCoverage.test.ts` asserts
that from the contract rather than from this list — including that the count is
still eleven, so adding a twelfth is noticed here rather than in whichever
assertion happens to fail. The four deferred rows are asserted ABSENT, which is
WP 4.2's exit check having a test before the package starts.

**The blind spot this table exposes, and it is not `graph_hash`'s:** the four
deferred tables are written by `calculate-network-science-metrics`,
`calculate-node-prominence` and `geocode-locations` over PostgREST, and because
they are outside the contract `dataPlaneAudit.test.ts` does not require audit
triggers on them — so those writes are not merely unattributed, they are
**unaudited, with nothing to notice**. That is D54 with names on it, and it is
WP 4.2's.

#### J · Baseline numbers

  - **326 tests**, 294 → 326. `graphHashCoverage.test.ts` is new (24); the audit

    goes 23 → 27, losing the `onConflict` assertion the key no longer needs and

  - **Ten rehearsal files**, green **all three ways** — fresh, over production's

  - **Nineteen mutations**, every one red with its own message, and one of them

  - `contract:check` green with **zero warnings**. R1 unchanged at 37/42/79 — this

  - `check:docs` green. No new TypeScript errors: 66 before, 66 after, identical

  - **Three §15 runs, none lost to the deploy race** (five were lost across the

#### K · §15, before and after — and the after-run could not tell whether the deploy landed

The before-run is section C's table and it is the reason the decision could be
made rather than reasoned about. It went out FIRST, in a push with no migration
in it, precisely so the three migration pushes could change none of the
trigger's three doors. **Zero runs lost to the race in this package**, against
five across the three before it.

**And then reading the after-run found a defect in this package's own probes.**
Every WP 4.1 count came back IDENTICAL to the before-run:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| live `proposals` grounded on a `graph_hash` | 0 | 0 |
| active `model_validations` cards | 0 | 0 |
| `project_memory` rows grounded on a hash | 0 | 0 |
| `simulation_runs` bound / gone | 17 / **0** | 17 / **0** |
| `bom_multi_level` · `customers` | 792 in 2 · 6 in 5 | unchanged |
| `hash_network`'s three tables | **0 · 0 · 0** | unchanged |
| data-plane rows with `actor_known: false` | 2 580 | 2 580 |

That is the CORRECT result for the data — nothing has run the moved paths and
nothing rewrites an audit row — and it is also exactly what a FAILED deploy
would have printed. The counts are about ROWS; the migrations changed FUNCTIONS
and added two COLUMNS, and §15's schema probe compares RELATIONS. **So the

Three probes close it, each a different claim, all three pushed to

domain_columns  2/2        wp41_functions  9/9
five projects   schema_version 2, inputs ✓ network ✓, both domain hashes compute

```

**`0 still matching` is the bump's whole visible effect as a number.** All six

### WP 4.2 — The analysis store · 2026-09-17 · `20260917000006`

#### A · The failing test, and it is D19 in one message

On `main`, against a real PostgreSQL 16:

```
analysis_get_or_start(project, 'network_metrics', {...}, 'nm@1', editor)
  → ERROR: WP 4.2 §1 — THERE IS NO ANALYSIS STORE.
```

`supabase/rehearsal/120` §1 was written to fail on exactly that before any of this
package existed, and its message says the defect rather than the symptom: there is
no table in which a completed analysis could be recognised a second time, so every
request recomputes and **nothing anywhere records that it did**.

**The store is an IDENTITY and the cache is a CONSEQUENCE**, which is the only
framing that makes a hit sound rather than a guess. The key is (project, kind,
`input_hash`, `params_hash`, `code_version`); two runs with the same key ARE the
same run by definition. That is why this package had to come after WP 4.1: without
a trust anchor that covers what the engine reads, `input_hash` would be a digest of
the wrong world and every hit would be a confident lie.

#### B · THE PREMISE CHECK — three inherited claims, and all three held

The brief said to check them rather than inherit them. Doing it cost under half an
hour and one of the three was worth the whole exercise:

  - **`graphHashCoverage.test.ts` really does assert the four DERIVED tables are
    ABSENT.** Verified by MUTATION, not by reading: adding a `network_nodes`
    `centrality` block to the snapshot's `network` domain turned it red with its own
    message (`network_nodes is an analysis OUTPUT and is inside the hash`) **and
    took two sibling assertions with it** — the "exactly three deep-tier tables"
    count and the column-membership check. A test that only one assertion guards is
    a test one refactor from silence; this one is guarded three ways.
  - **`hash_network` covers exactly `tier2_suppliers`, `tier3_suppliers`,
    `multi_tier_supply_chain`** — confirmed in `20260917000002:218-256`. Still zero
    rows in production.
  - **`main` is green on `data contract` at `06626c8`** — run `35227049832`,
    success.

#### C · D12's EVIDENCE WAS STALE, AND THE ROW WAS WRONG ABOUT WHICH HALF

The brief flagged the citation and it was right to. §4 D12 cited
`20250925164454_…sql:39-52`; the live definition is
`20260712110000_network_metrics_check_performance.sql`, a `CREATE OR REPLACE` by a
package this plan does not contain. **So one half was fixed by work the plan cannot
see** — which is exactly the "fact with no owner" §4 exists to prevent.

**The second half was checked by MEASUREMENT rather than by reading**, because
reading is how the row got wrong in the first place. Both definitions were built
side by side on a real PostgreSQL 16 and run over the full 8-case matrix
(`supply_chain_data` × fresher BOM × node metrics):

```
8 cases: needs_recalculation differs in 0, data_last_modified differs in 2
```

**`needs_recalculation` is identical in all eight.** The old version can NEVER
wrongly answer "up to date", because that answer requires `has_metrics`, which
requires `supply_chain_data` to be non-empty — which is precisely the condition
under which the cartesian `FROM` produces rows and its MAXes are correct. The two
cases that differ are `data_last_modified`, which the old version reports as
**1970-01-01** for a project with empty `supply_chain_data` however fresh its BOM
and lane tables are.

So: the cartesian half was real and is closed; the "up to date" half was
mis-stated, and the true defect underneath it — an epoch timestamp returned to
every caller on a pre-combine project — is closed by the same rewrite, **whose own
header claims "index-friendly rewrites with identical semantics".** The semantics
differ in exactly those two cases, in the direction of correctness. A fix nobody
recorded as a fix.

The function is deprecated IN PLACE (`auto_calculate_network_metrics_on_completion`
still calls it on every completion flip) with a `COMMENT ON FUNCTION` naming D12,
and §8 of the rehearsal fails if it is dropped or if the comment stops naming D12.

#### D · THE D56 DECISION, WHICH IS A SPLIT AND NOT A TIER

Three packages deferred this with the same sentence. The reason it survived is that
the honest answer is uncomfortable: **`network_nodes` is BOTH.** Eight columns an
analysis wrote (`prominence`, `prominence_updated_at`, five centralities,
`network_metrics_updated_at`) beside nine a user uploaded (`uid`, `depth`, `name`,
`country`, `industry`, `website`, `traded_as`, `revenue`, `lat`, `long`, `is_seed`).
`node_list` is the same shape. That is D19 in one table, and it is why "what tier is
it" has no answer while the table is one thing.

**Decision: the answer is a SPLIT, and WP 4.3 executes it. Written down with the
reason, because "we deferred it again" is what three packages already said.** Three
things have to be true first and none of them is true today:

  1. **The computed half has nowhere to go until the analyzers dual-write.** §11
     gives that to WP 4.3 and tells this package not to migrate a reader. Splitting
     first means a migration moving columns no writer targets.
  2. **The input half cannot be described until it has a natural key — and it does
     not have one. That is D72**, found while enumerating this blast radius.
  3. **Describing the input half is a second `schema_version` bump.** WP 4.1's rule
     is "every value column of every tier-2 input table", so the coverage gate folds
     it into `hash_network` the moment the sidecar exists. §16 · WP 4.1 · C is what
     one bump costs, and D70 is what it costs on a day the proposal count is not
     zero.

**The blast radius, enumerated so WP 4.3 inherits it** (also in §4 D56). Writers of
the input half: `UploadWizard.tsx:1024` (`bulk_insert_network_nodes`), `:1079`
(`bulk_insert_network_edges`), `combine-project/index.ts:468,477`
(`refresh_node_list_for_project`). **`bulk_insert_network_summary` exists and has no
caller at all** — which is why `network_summary` holds 0 rows while its two inputs
hold 3 514. Writers of the computed half:
`calculate-network-science-metrics/index.ts:132`,
`calculate-node-prominence/index.ts:111`, `geocode-locations/index.ts:245,292`.
Readers of both halves as one row: `ProjectDataViewer.tsx`, `FirmLevelNetwork.tsx`
(`prominence`), `DataManager.tsx` (`is_critical_node`, `critical_node_score`),
`MapView.tsx`, `verifiableExports.ts`. All four bulk RPCs remain tier-2-skipping and
unaudited.

#### E · D72 — AN UPSERT ON A CONSTRAINT THAT DOES NOT EXIST

Enumerating that blast radius turned up a live defect.
`calculate-network-science-metrics/index.ts:114-115` calls
`.upsert(upsertRows, { onConflict: 'project_id,uid' })` on the fallback path — the
one that derives a graph from `supply_chain_data` when the network tables are empty
and must create node rows before metrics can be stored against them.
**`network_nodes` has no unique index on `(project_id, uid)`.** Its only uniqueness
is the surrogate `network_nodes_pkey`. Confirmed against a real database rather than
inferred:

```
ERROR: there is no unique or exclusion constraint matching the ON CONFLICT specification
```

The handler is `console.error(...)` with no throw and no early return, so the
function proceeds to a per-node `.update()` loop that matches zero rows, and reports
success. **A project whose nodes exist only via that fallback gets no metrics and no
error anybody sees.**

This is D5's class arriving in the deferred group, and the reason `natural-key` (I4)
being MET does not cover it is that I4 and R5 are scoped to tier-2 tables IN THE
CONTRACT. `network_nodes` is deferred, so R5 has never looked at it — **D54's
qualifier doing damage in a second place, which is the argument for R11 stated as a
live bug rather than as a principle.**

#### F · D54 — THE RULE, AND WHY IT IS NOT A GATE ON BEING AUDITED

`contract:check` **R11**: every deferred table must appear in its group's `audited:`
map, and the declaration must match the triggers the migrations create — read from
the same `auditedTables()` R9 uses, so the two halves of the same fact have one
source (I1). It lives where R1 already reads `coverage.yaml`, not in a comment,
which is what §11 asked for. Mutation-tested both ways: a table dropped from the map
fails, and a table declaring `audited: true` with no trigger fails naming the
disagreement.

**It deliberately does NOT require `true`.** 42 of 42 deferred tables are unaudited,
so a gate would be red on arrival and unlandable — the same reasoning that made WP
4.1's writer list a ratchet. The rule requires the SENTENCE: `false` has to be typed
by a person, beside the package that owns fixing it, and R11 prints the count every
run so it cannot quietly grow.

**And the deferral list itself was making decisions nobody had made.**
`model_validations` and `external_evidence` were in the WP 4.2 group — the first
because it has "validation" in its name, the second because nobody had looked at it.
`model_validations` already carries `graph_hash`, `policy_hash`, `scenario_hash` and
`engine_fingerprint`; its whole subject is staleness, so it is WP 4.4's.
`external_evidence` is the agent's evidence store and belongs with the decision
plane, WP 6.1's. Both moved, with the reason written in the file. That regrouping is
D54's own thesis applied to D54's own list.

#### G · THE MUTATIONS, AND THE TWO THAT SURVIVED

**Twenty-one mutations, every one finally red with its own message. Two were GREEN
first, and both were defects in the TEST:**

  - **the audit assertion could not tell which STATEMENT wrote the row.** Removing
    the `analysis_runs` INSERT trigger left §5 green, because
    `analysis_complete_run`'s UPDATE writes an `analysis_runs` audit row too and an
    untyped `count(*)` cannot distinguish them. The claim is that CLAIMING a run is
    audited, so the assertion now names `action = 'insert'` — and a second
    assertion covers `analysis_results` on its own statement.
  - **`analysis_results` had no per-entity uniqueness and nothing noticed.** The
    mutation that downgraded the index stayed green because
    `analysis_complete_run` refuses a second completion, so no test reached the
    duplicate. §10 now attempts the direct INSERT a future writer would make.

**The two mutations that stayed GREEN for WP 4.1 both fire here** (§16 · WP 4.1 ·
E): removing `set_config` from `assert_writer_may_act`, and making it keep whatever
the session already held. The whole file is one transaction and
`set_config(..., true)` is transaction-local, so every call is preceded by setting
`app.current_user_id` to a DIFFERENT user and the message names the poison. An
assertion that cannot fail is the failure mode this plan keeps rediscovering; the
rule that catches it is not "be careful", it is *run the mutation, and when it does
not fire, the test is what is wrong.*

**And a mutation run left a trap that caught the next tool.** The concurrency check
reported TWO runs on one key on its first execution and looked like a genuine
defect. It was not: `contract:rehearse` leaves its database behind, and the database
still held the mutant schema from the previous round, where the key index had been
downgraded on purpose. The script had faithfully measured a mutant and would have
reported it as the product. It now refuses to run unless
`analysis_runs_key_uniq` is both unique and partial — **the same failure mode as a
scan that finds nothing and passes, which is why the guard is a hard exit and not a
warning.**

#### H · GAP CHECK — concurrency, from two real sessions

§11 asks whether two parallel requests on a COLD key create two runs. **They create
one.** `npm run contract:concurrency`:

```
✓ session B BLOCKED on A's uncommitted key (1453 ms)
✓ two parallel requests on a cold key created exactly ONE run (got 1)
✓ both sessions were handed the SAME run id
✓ an unfinished claim is NOT reported as a cache hit
✓ once the winner completes, the next request is a HIT
✓ still exactly ONE run after four requests (got 1)
```

**Not assertable in one transaction, and the file says why**: inside a single
session the second call sees the first one's uncommitted row through its own
snapshot, so the race cannot happen and a single-transaction assertion would answer
a different question while wearing this one's label. Session A holds its transaction
open across a `pg_sleep` so B's claim is GUARANTEED to arrive inside the window
rather than hoped to — and B's 1 453 ms is asserted, because a B that returned
immediately never overlapped and would make everything below it meaningless.

**What serialises them is the unique index, not the lookup.** The `SELECT` is not a
lock and on a cold key both sessions miss it; `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` returns
NOTHING to the loser rather than raising, which is how it learns to read the winner's
row. The mutation that drops `ON CONFLICT` turns it into a duplicate-key error, and
the mutation that removes the unique index produces two runs.

#### I · THE DEVIATION FROM §11, AND WHY

§11 wrote the key as a flat `UNIQUE (project_id, analysis_kind, input_hash,
params_hash, code_version)`. **Taken literally, the first FAILED attempt owns that
key forever**: the retry cannot insert, so an analysis that crashed once can never
run again on that input — a permanently poisoned cache entry with no exit that does
not delete history, and the store never deletes. The index is partial,
`WHERE status <> 'failed'`. §11 is edited in this commit to say so, §9 of the
rehearsal asserts both halves, and the mutation restoring the flat index turns it
red with the poisoned key visible in the message.

The before-run (`35229431958`) measured two things nothing had ever measured.

| table | rows | projects | rows with a COMPUTED column |
|---|---|---|---|
| `node_list` | **1 747** | **7** | 0 |
| `network_nodes` | **1 385** | 1 | **1 385** |

**5 261 rows, 1 385 carrying a computed column, and NONE carrying an input hash.**

#### L · D73 — THE THIRD MODE EARNED ITS KEEP, AGAIN

The brief says to run `--since HEAD` before every push because it builds the shape
`main` meets after the merge and no other mode does. It caught something.

`supabase/rehearsal/120` §8 asserts that `should_recalculate_network_metrics`
carries a comment naming D12. **Green fresh, green over production's shape, RED on
`--since HEAD`:**

```
WP 4.2 §8 — the deprecation carries no comment naming D12. Comment is: (none)
```

The first two modes build the base from the BASE branch's artifact and then RUN
this branch's migration, so the `COMMENT ON FUNCTION` is applied by the statement
itself. The third executes the artifact THIS branch WROTE — and the artifact did
not have the comment, because `introspect.mjs` matched
`COMMENT ON (TABLE|COLUMN|VIEW|FUNCTION|…)` and then recorded the text **for TABLE
alone**, every other target falling through the same `return`. So the function
records had no `comment`, `emitFunctions` had nothing to emit, and a base rebuilt
from the artifact had functions stripped of their documentation with nothing to
notice.

**That is D52's class precisely**, and it had D52's signature: two green modes and
one red. The fix records the comment against the signature when the statement
spells the arguments and against the bare name otherwise, and emits every
`COMMENT ON FUNCTION` AFTER all bodies — because a comment may live in a different
migration from its `CREATE` (this one does: the body is `20260712110000`, the
comment `20260917000006`), so unlike the body it cannot be replayed from the
defining file. 16 functions carry one today.

A quieter second half came with it: `CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION` rebuilt the
artifact record from scratch, so replacing a function would have dropped a comment
an EARLIER migration had set — although PostgreSQL preserves it across a replace.
The artifact now carries it forward, which is the artifact agreeing with the
database rather than with the statement it last read.

#### M · D74 — THE PAGES WERE WRONG ABOUT THE INVARIANT THEY REPORT

Reading the page this package's own sidecar generated turned up a third finding.
`docs/data/tables/analysis_runs.md` said:

> **Intended natural key:** … the key this table's grain implies and the database
> does NOT enforce today.

…about a key `supabase/rehearsal/120` §9 had just finished proving the database
DOES enforce. The sentence was unconditional in `renderKeys`. It was accurate when
WP 1.4 wrote it; **WP 3.3 made it false the day it created the seven unique
indexes**, and nothing noticed because `natural_key_intended` legitimately STAYS on
a table whose key has landed — R5's second half compares the landed columns against
it, so the field is load-bearing and only the prose was wrong.

**Eleven of the thirteen pages carrying that field published the opposite of the
truth**; two (`projects`, `risk_data`) were correct. The subject is
`natural-key` (I4) — the invariant those pages exist to report — and the audience is
a user deciding whether re-uploading a file will duplicate their rows.

**This is D40 again**: a generated page stating a fact the schema had moved on from,
generated and CI-gated so it stays true-looking indefinitely. T5 says transparency
survives handover *because* it is generated; D40 and D74 are the same reminder that
a generated falsehood also survives handover. The fix is conditional prose that
names the constraint when the key is landed. The field, and therefore R5, is
untouched.

#### N · The caveat, and what WP 4.3 should not inherit as settled

  - **Nothing has ever called `analysis_get_or_start` outside a rehearsal.** Every
    claim about a cache hit is a claim about `supabase/rehearsal/` fixtures. The
    after-run asserts the TABLES AND FUNCTIONS are present in production — not that
    anything used them — because WP 4.1's after-run could not distinguish a landed
    deploy from a failed one and every count came back identical.
  - **`analysis_kind` is open, and "open" has a cost nobody has paid yet.** The
    CHECK constrains the shape; the catalog lives in the sidecar. Nothing yet
    verifies that a kind a CALLER passes exists in that catalog, because there are
    no callers. The first one should bring that gate with it.
  - **The four deferred tables are still written by the four bulk RPCs**, still
    tier-2-skipping, still unaudited. This package described none of them on
    purpose (section D); WP 4.3 inherits the enumerated radius and D72 as its first
    step.
  - **`audit-actor` (G4) is still NOT met** and this package did not move it. D71's
    26 stand at 26; the two new writers were built attributed rather than added to
    the debt.
